newsitem.title: USA: Baseball players, owners see progress on antitrust.
newsitem.headline: Baseball players, owners see progress on antitrust.

text.p: Baseball's Major League owners and players have agreed on a proposal to partially reform the game's 75-year-old exemption from antitrust laws, Senate Judiciary Committee chairman Orrin Hatch said Tuesday.

The two sides agreed to their own, narrower alternative to a bill introduced by Hatch, a Utah Republican. His bill would make antitrust legislation apply to Major League baseball, as it does to other professional sports, but not to minor league baseball.
Hatch said he and other committee members would have to examine the alternative language that mostly applies to antitrust exemptions as they apply to labour.

But he said, "I think it is safe to say that the most important impediment to passage of baseball antitrust reform has been elminated, and that it is truly a momentous occasion when Major League Baseball owners have aligned in support of such reform."

Hatch said he had gotten a letter from acting baseball commissioner Bud Selig, who did not attended the Judiciary hearing Tuesday and did not send a representative. Donald Fehr, executive director of the Major League Players Association, did attend and also said both sides had agreed.
Among other things, the antitrust exemption now bars players from lodging unfair labour complaints with the National Labour Relations Board.

Hatch has been working on this issue since a players' strike led to the cancellation of the World Series in 1994. His bill is named for the late Curt Flood, a star outfielder with the St. Louis Cardinals in the 1960s who went to court rather than be traded to Philadelphia without his consent.
Flood lost that initial challenge but paved the way for other action to elminate baseball's reserve clause and let players move from team to team as free agents.
